 CONFESSIONS
 The Body ’s Sara Boustany and Kristina Bogic on Kissing Girls and Keeping Secrets
 By Interview 
 Photographed by Myles Pettengill 
 November 16, 2026
 “Everybody start kissing,” Sara Boustany admits to thinking during her first watch of Netflix’s new must-see TV show, The Body. The actress plays Elise Zakaria, a bitch with a heart of gold, in Quinn Shephard ’s sapphic, psychological thriller set at a Northeast Catholic high school in the early aughts. The genre-bending series centers around a girls dance troupe that start having strange religious hallucinations following an initiation-mishap. Drugs, Satan, and lesbians— The Body is a coming-of-age story unlike you’ve ever seen. And according to the actresses, the process of making the show also possessed a cult-ish undertone. “Everyone’s getting sick and you’re in sub-40 degrees and they’re like, ’We’re going to put you in this little bikini,’” confesses Kristina Bogic , who plays Anya Butler on the show—the dance team captain and Elise’s other half. Ahead of the show’s release, with Boustany calling from Mexico and Bogic from Australia, the pair braved a 17-hour time difference to discuss slickbacks, dance rehearsals, and magical thinking.—ISABELLA SOCCI
 MONDAY 6PM OCTOBER 19, 2026 MEXICO 
 ———
 SARA BOUSTANY: Sorry, I’m in Mexico right now in the middle of nowhere. Are you in Australia? 
 KRISTINA BOGIC: I’m in Australia now. I went on a little trip. 
 BOUSTANY: Where was your little trip? 
 BOGIC: Hamilton Island. It’s in the north of Australia, this little island where you can only drive around on golf buggies. 
 BOUSTANY: That’s so cute. 
 BOGIC: What are you doing in Mexico? 
 BOUSTANY: Just for a vacation. 
 BOGIC: Beautiful. Do you want to talk about our audition experience? 
 BOUSTANY: I’m down. Everybody had a crazy experience getting the role. 
 BOGIC: It’s all weirdly a little spiritual as well. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, for sure. You go first. 
 BOGIC: Okay. I got the original audition, I think a few months before I even got a callback. It was a really long audition process for me. I did the first audition, I did a callback, and then I didn’t hear back for maybe a month or so. I was like, “You know what? I’m going to go to Europe with my best friend.” I was at this tiny, little airport and I got a call from my agent saying, “Hey, you need to get on this callback. It’s with Sara.” And I remember looking Sara up and going, “Oh my god.” 
 BOUSTANY: Oh, stop it. 
 BOGIC: And then we did maybe four— 
 BOUSTANY: We did three. Was it four? I thought it was three. 
 BOGIC: Maybe. 
 BOUSTANY: Maybe your auditions were different. 
 BOGIC: I did one with Geena [Meszaros] too, who plays Lisbeth. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, I did too. With Anya, it was a long process for me, but I remember it so vividly. Do you? 
 BOGIC: Yeah, I remember it really well. 
 BOUSTANY: You had your hair back in a little pony and you were in Italy, right? 
 BOGIC: Yeah, I was in Italy, in Taormina. They were like, “Can you slick back your hair and wear no makeup for the audition?” Then, I wake up and I’m slicked back. For half of the auditions I was traveling around and it was at 3:00 AM for me because of the different time zones. 
 BOUSTANY: That’s crazy. 
 BOGIC: I was in the most random hotels. My best friend who traveled with me, she’s like, “I watched a tiny clip of the show. I remember this script so well from how many times I was doing it.” 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, my friends as well. I had a couple of my friends audition too. 
 BOGIC: I actually knew a lot of people that auditioned for this. I remember getting lunch with some of my actor friends in Melbourne and they were all like, “Oh, there’s this open call for T he Body .” As soon as I heard about it, I wanted it immediately. 
 BOUSTANY: Me too. But wait, we’re getting sidetracked.  
 BOGIC: Let me ask you the proper questions. Can we talk about our rehearsal period and how we all got close? Because it was eight weeks of dance rehearsals.  
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, there was a really intense week where it was every day, every day, every day. I really think each of us was almost hospitalized at a certain point. 
 BOGIC: We had Ryan Heffington putting us through boot camp. He was so patient, so graceful and kind when we were all getting to know each other. There was so much energy, but I’m so happy we all had that time because it warmed us up to each other. 
 BOUSTANY: It really did. 
 BOGIC: I’ve made a point in every interview or conversation I’ve had about the show to say it has never once felt competitive. You’re coming into a group of 12 young girls and it was honestly the most supportive environment. 
 BOUSTANY: It really was. We just bonded so quickly. I’d never experienced something like that. I just feel so happy and proud to be a part of a group of girls who just love each other. It’s not rare. Women are amazing. But it’s rare in a workplace to be so close. 
 BOGIC: Yeah. As coworkers, you’re all put together and they’re like, “Okay, now be friends.” And it’s always a little awkward, but we all just clicked. 
 BOUSTANY: I have a question for you. How did you decompress after a disturbing or challenging scene? 
 BOGIC: I was going to literally ask you this. 
 BOUSTANY: Well, you had more of those, so you should answer it. 
 BOGIC: Honestly, at the beginning, I was very good at shaking off whatever scene I had to do that day. But there were times, I don’t know if you remember, I was in the trenches. 
 BOUSTANY: What do you mean, do I remember? I was traumatized for you. It was crazy. We were in the freezing cold. 
 BOGIC: If I’d had one moment of sun throughout the entire six months of filming, it would’ve saved me. But imagine you’re always together. It’s a huge group. It’s a huge crew. Everyone’s getting sick, and you’re in sub-40-degree weather, and they’re like, “We’re going to put you in this little bikini, and you’re going to walk around.” 
 BOUSTANY: And then also cry and lose your mind. 
 BOGIC: How to decompress? On the weekend, I would just rot away, but I needed that. I needed time to not speak, to not be touched or anything, and just fade away. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah. I don’t think the show would’ve even been what it was if none of us leaned on each other as much. 
 BOGIC: Yeah. Even when it comes to press stuff, I’m so thankful I get to do it. We’re very lucky. Every time I’m with you guys, I’m like, “I’m safe.” 
 BOUSTANY: I know. 
 BOGIC: Okay. I’m going to ask you a question. What was your high school experience like? 
 BOUSTANY: I truly blocked a lot of it out. I didn’t have a negative experience. Emotions are so heightened when you’re a teenager and your body processes it as some kind of trauma, so it gets stored away. 
 BOGIC: Everything feels amplified at that age as well. Any experience I had with school was not a good one at all. 
 BOUSTANY: Really? 
 BOGIC: I was homeschooled from seventh grade, and then when I got to tenth grade, I went to an art school for three weeks. Imagine those formative years not growing up in a school system. You can go to the bathroom whenever you want. You’re treated like an adult in society because there’s not this hierarchy. When I went back to that, it shook me so much, and I ended up just leaving school. It was the best thing I could have done. If you give teenage girls the chance to just figure out what they want to do and who they want to be, they’re not going to waste that chance. That’s when we have the most excitement for life and innocence about the world. I’m very lucky I had those years to figure out what I wanted to do with my life. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah. I also barely went because freshman year was just hell mentally for no reason. So for half of that semester, I was homeschooled. I went back sophomore year, and then I went to Lebanon, and then the revolution happened, and then none of us were going to school for six months. Got back to L.A., COVID hit, no school. I spent senior year at a normal school. I feel like my life just started a couple years ago. 
 BOGIC: We’re both very lucky we had enough time to figure our shit out. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah. My parents were extremely supportive, and I wouldn’t have been able to figure out what I wanted to do without them. 
 BOGIC: Me too. What was your first impression of me? Tell me everything. 
 BOUSTANY: At first, you were pretty reserved and I loved it. I had an immediate connection with you. When we first met, we were doing dance stuff. I remember glancing at you and then you would glance at me and then we’d just be like— 
 BOGIC: I couldn’t believe everyone was real.  Imagine walking into a room of 12 of the most beautiful women you’ve ever seen. 
 BOUSTANY: Literally. 
 BOGIC: When we started filming, Geena and I had a conversation. We were like, “Isn’t Sara so amazing? She’s so amazing. Everything she does.” Whenever I was in a scene with you, I was like, “Girl, I got to fucking bring it.” 
 BOUSTANY: Oh, that’s so sweet. I love that. We only had one audition scene and I thought our chemistry was so amazing. But I was just curious about how you were going to play Anya because we talked so much about her bad decision making. I was curious about how you were going to bring that warmth to her, and I really felt it. What’s funny is that the only thing we would bicker about on set was Anya and Elise, but now we’re so on the same page about them. 
 BOGIC: But you know what? That’s such a good sign that we both trusted and believed in our characters so much. You would be able to feel it instantly watching the show if I couldn’t justify one of Anya’s decisions. I had to defend her through everything. 
 BOUSTANY: We’re in pretty bad shape most of the season. Someone asked me, “What do you think Anya and Elise love about each other?” And I’m like, “We didn’t even have the chance to explore their relationship outside of something happening so abruptly.” 
 BOGIC: Yeah. You see their dynamic as friends, but I would love to see Anya and Elise have more best friend moments. You get a sense of it in episode one, but once you see a lot of the issues in the show and how they talk, you can tell they’re very comfortable with each other.  
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, it was the girlness and the gossip of them. I don’t even know what the word is. It’s the conspiring that all girls love to do.  
 BOGIC: What should we talk about next? Do you have any superstitions? Irrational fears? Psychic experiences? Do you believe in curses? Astrology? 
 BOUSTANY: It’s more so words having power and what you put out is what you get. I’m going to get real vulnerable right now. When you’re struggling so much with yourself, sometimes you just want to talk about it to the people you care about. But when you tell people something they start focusing on it. So basically, keep what you doubt about yourself to yourself, because what you put out is what people will inevitably feel. 
 BOGIC: Not putting weight behind words is a big thing, which is basically just what you’re saying. I’m an anxious person in general, and as soon as I tell someone I’m anxious, all of a sudden it’s ten times worse. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, but it needs to be a specific person, because I remember talking to Geena about this and telling her something that was upsetting me. She was just like, “I see you being upset and it makes me feel like you’re human.” I guess it’s kind of superstitious of me to feel that way. I have random ones as well. My OCD comes out in random things, like clenching my teeth for a certain amount of time. 
 BOGIC: Yeah. This isn’t a superstition. This is weird shit that I do. If I’m eating and I only chew on one side of my mouth, I have to even it out with the other side. It’s a sensory thing. You know what? Say I do an audition and I really want it, I used to manifest and smother it with my hopes and dreams.  I’d put all of my energy into it, and then I felt like I wouldn’t get the role because I would suffocate it. As soon as I let them go, they’d come back to me. I’m like, “Okay, I’m very grateful for this,” but I try not to invest so much spiritual energy into it.  
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, The Body felt that way for me. 
 BOGIC: I think if I didn’t get T he Body , I would’ve dwindled away. I was so obsessed with Anya. I would’ve been heartbroken if I didn’t get her. 
 BOUSTANY: Oh my god, I would’ve lost my fucking mind. 
 BOGIC: I can’t even imagine my life without meeting everyone. It’s not even something I can fathom. 
 BOUSTANY: Me too. Sometimes you feel like these things were bound to happen. Sometimes I’m just like, “I knew that it was going to happen for me,” but it happens and then you’re, like, imposter syndrome to the fucking max. Would you have been friends with the characters in high school? 
 BOGIC: I feel like Anya would’ve been the girl to be like, “Have you ever made out with girls?” And I would’ve been like, “Girl, okay, I know where this is going.” Or I would’ve shaken her a couple times. [Laughs] 
 BOUSTANY: I would’ve been friends with Elise for sure, but this bitchy defense mechanism—cut it out. You have a good sense of yourself. You do not need to be doing all that. But it’s funny, I would. 
 BOGIC: But you know what? I think you thought that about Elise as well. And I think it’s good that you did because you made her so much softer than I ever read her on the page. I think she was always going to be lovable because she’s witty and funny and cheeky. But you gave her such a soft little heart where you’re, like, baby Elise. You just want to hold her. 
 BOUSTANY: Nobody’s a bitch just because they’re a bitch. It’s always something. Like an unrequited love. 
 BOGIC: Oh. Well, yes. I have no idea what you’re talking about. [Laughs] 
 BOUSTANY: I would’ve been friends with Anya. 
 BOGIC: Me too. I would love to explore her funny, girly side because I didn’t get to explore that as much. I did with Lisbeth a little bit too. 
 BOUSTANY: True. 
 BOGIC: What I love is that although our trope is focused on, there are so many relationships in the show that I really root for. Not always romantically, but platonically. 
 BOUSTANY: I like everyone to be romantic. 
 BOGIC: Everyone’s romantic. 
 BOUSTANY: I’m like, “Everyone, start kissing now.” 
 BOGIC: The first time we watched it, we were like, “Smash, smash. I want these two together. Everyone has chemistry.” 
 BOUSTANY: Kind of wish Lisbeth and Anya kissed really quickly. 
 BOGIC: Just really quick? 
 BOUSTANY: Just really quick, and then nobody ever talked about it ever again. 
 BOGIC: That would be a Lisbeth thing to do. She’d come up and kiss Anya as a threat. 
 BOUSTANY: She totally would. I love Lisbeth. 
 BOGIC: Me too. She’s probably one of my favorite characters. 
 BOUSTANY: Are you good at keeping secrets? 
 BOGIC: You are not good at keeping secrets. It eats you up inside. 
 BOUSTANY: No, I’m not. If I feel guilty about something, I can’t do it. But if it’s a secret that I’m keeping and it doesn’t hurt anybody, my lips are sealed. 
 BOGIC: I tell everyone everything. Ever since I was little, even people I don’t know very well have told me their deepest, darkest secrets. 
 BOUSTANY: Me too. I think it’s because we are very vulnerable with people. 
 BOGIC: True. I don’t remember the last time I lied. You know what? I exaggerate stories.  
 BOUSTANY: Really? 
 BOGIC: Not big things, but if it’s something funny, somehow the story gets bigger and bigger each time. But I’m like, “I’m an actor. That’s reasonable.” 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah, that is reasonable. Everybody’s lied. But I believe in confessing for sure. This is maybe controversial, but if someone tells me something fucked up, I’m like, “Okay, you better tell them before I do.”  
 BOGIC: Yeah. If I feel guilt for holding a secret, it makes me feel sick. I can’t keep it in. But I’m like Anya in that way where it literally will eat me up inside until I crack, and then I’m like, “Ugh, this is it.” And I just vomit it out. 
 BOUSTANY: Yeah. It’s weird. I can’t do it. 
 BOGIC: Me neither.
